title: The Afternoon Brief: College Bans Collide With Court Orders; NFL Braces for Cutdown Chaos
dek: The Big Ten and SEC have issued eligibility bans on players with professional experience, but a Louisiana court order explicitly allows some of those same players to return. The colliding authorities converge on August 31, when an injunction hearing and NFL roster cutdowns will test who controls college football eligibility.
author: GoCheckMySports
key_fact: Conferences and courts are on a collision course. The Big Ten and SEC banned players with professional contracts or roster experience effective immediately, but those players already hold state court orders allowing their return. The August 31 hearing will determine whether judicial relief or conference rules prevail, and the NFL's roster cutdowns that same week will likely produce more players seeking court relief.
bottom_line: College conferences and a state court are now in direct conflict over player eligibility, with both the Big Ten and SEC banning professional-experience players effective immediately even as those same athletes hold court orders allowing their return. The August 31 injunction hearing and concurrent NFL roster cutdowns will test whether judicial relief can override conference rules, and the week will likely generate more players seeking court intervention. Meanwhile, the NFL approved a league-record $9.612 billion Seahawks sale, ended the Pro Bowl after 80 years, and absorbed training-camp injuries to key position players as the regular season approaches.
body: The Big Ten voted unanimously on Tuesday to prohibit football players who have signed professional contracts, appeared on professional rosters, or declared for the NFL Draft as underclassmen without withdrawing from maintaining eligibility for college competition. The SEC announced an identical football policy that same evening and extended the ban to men's and women's basketball players with NBA and WNBA experience. Both conferences acted in direct response to a Louisiana state court's temporary restraining order issued last week that allowed a group of players who participated in NFL training camp and preseason to return to college.

The rules now collide head-on with judicial authority. The Louisiana court ruled in favor of those returning players on the grounds that they would not have entered the professional process had they known college eligibility would remain available. That temporary restraining order extends until a full injunction hearing on August 31, the same day the NFL will conduct its roster cutdowns. The SEC has announced it can impose penalties on member institutions that sign ineligible players, but it remains unclear how conferences will enforce bans when players hold active court orders permitting their participation. How LSU proceeds with players named Wright and Harris will reveal whether courts or conferences retain authority over college football eligibility.

The NCAA, which called such rulings "destabilizing," faces its own authority questions as it navigates conflicting judicial and institutional mandates. The August 31 roster cutdown will likely generate additional players seeking court relief, expanding the set of athletes challenging conference eligibility rules. The reporting does not detail what specific enforcement mechanisms the conferences plan to deploy or whether they will attempt to enjoin the court's order.

Elsewhere, the NFL's professional landscape shifted with the league's unanimous approval of the $9.612 billion Seahawks sale to the Khosla family, the largest franchise transaction in NFL history. The deal is slated to close in September and ends nearly three decades of ownership by the Paul Allen estate. The league also eliminated the Pro Bowl after nearly 80 years, replacing the televised all-star game with a recognition-only honor bestowed on 88 selected players. Viewership had collapsed from 6.7 million in 2023 to 1.9 million in 2026.

In injuries, Calvin Austin, the Giants' starting slot receiver, suffered an apparent serious knee injury without contact during Tuesday practice. His knee buckled while running a 1-on-1 route against cornerback Deonte Banks. The status and full severity of the injury remain unconfirmed pending official medical evaluation. The Ravens placed center Danny Pinter on injured reserve after he tore his patellar tendon during a joint practice with Minnesota, sidelining him for the entire 2026 season. Pinter was competing to start after signing with Baltimore in free agency.

The WNBA's Fever-Sky game on NBC and Peacock drew 3.31 million viewers, the most-watched regular-season game since the league's opening weekend in 1997. Chicago won 113-90. The game was marked by an altercation late in the third quarter when fan Enes Kanter Freedom was ejected after a verbal exchange with Sky guard Natasha Cloud. Accounts of what sparked the confrontation differ: Sky owner Michael Alter said Freedom stepped toward Cloud after she laid up and spoke toward him; courtside fan Trista Smith told reporters Freedom did not initiate the altercation. The Sky has placed an indefinite ban on Freedom attending home games, though a league source said he is not banned from other WNBA venues and the league does not intend a league-wide ban.

In other moves, DeWanna Bonner signed with the Atlanta Dream following a buyout from the Phoenix Mercury, joining Angel Reese for the playoff stretch. Jonathan Kuminga agreed to a two-year, $13 million contract with the Minnesota Timberwolves as an unrestricted free agent. Liverpool agreed to pay just over 100 million pounds guaranteed for France winger Bradley Barcola from PSG, with add-ons worth approximately 20 million pounds, a compromise from PSG's initial 145 million pound ask.

Unrivaled, the women's 3-on-3 basketball league, announced a Series C funding round valuing the company at $650 million, nearly double its $340 million valuation from September. Players hold approximately 30% of the company, valued at nearly $200 million.
